overview: North Korea is a country in East Asia, on the northern half of the Korean Peninsula. Its capital and largest city is Pyongyang. Korea was divided after the Second World War, and the Korean War of 1950–53 ended with a ceasefire but no peace treaty. North Korea is ruled by a single party led by one family, and it is one of the most closed-off countries in the world.

geography.text: North Korea is mostly mountainous, with narrow coastal plains along the Yellow Sea to the west and the Sea of Japan to the east. Mount Paektu, a volcano on the border with China, is its highest peak. The Yalu and Tumen rivers form most of its northern border.

subsections.title: Climate
subsections.text: Very cold winters and hot, rainy summers.

subsections.title: Wildlife
subsections.text: Red-crowned cranes and other birds use the demilitarised zone as a wildlife refuge.

history.text: Korea was united for centuries under kingdoms such as Goryeo and Joseon, then ruled by Japan from 1910 to 1945. After the Second World War the north was occupied by the Soviet Union and the south by the United States. Kim Il Sung founded North Korea in 1948 and invaded the South in 1950, starting the Korean War. His family has ruled ever since, and the country has developed nuclear weapons.

events.title: North Korea founded
events.text: Kim Il Sung becomes leader of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea.

events.title: Armistice
events.text: Fighting stops, but no peace treaty is signed.

events.title: Nuclear test
events.text: North Korea carries out its first nuclear test.

government.text: North Korea is a one-party dictatorship ruled by the Kim family since its founding in 1948. Kim Jong Un has led the country since 2011. Elections offer only one candidate. It is one of the most isolated countries in the world and has developed nuclear weapons and long-range missiles.

economy.text: North Korea has a state-controlled economy and is one of the poorest countries in Asia. Most of its trade is with China. International sanctions over its weapons programmes limit its exports. Severe famine killed hundreds of thousands of people in the 1990s.

culture.text: North Korea's culture is shaped by state ideology and huge shows of loyalty to its leaders, such as the Mass Games, in which tens of thousands of people perform in synchronised displays. Ordinary citizens have almost no access to the internet or foreign media.

items.title: Mass Games
items.text: Huge displays with tens of thousands of performers.

items.title: Pyongyang
items.text: A planned capital with grand monuments.

subsections.title: Food
subsections.text: Naengmyeon, cold buckwheat noodles, and kimchi.

subsections.title: Music and arts
subsections.text: Large-scale performances and state-approved music and film.

subsections.title: Traditions and festivals
subsections.text: The Lunar New Year and Chuseok harvest festival are family holidays.

sport.text: Football, weightlifting and gymnastics are North Korea's strongest sports. Its men's team reached the World Cup quarter-finals in 1966, beating Italy, and its women's team has won the Asian Cup and youth world titles.

items.text: Beat Italy to reach the World Cup quarter-finals.

items.title: Weightlifting
items.text: North Korea has won several Olympic weightlifting golds.

didYouKnow: North and South Korea never signed a peace treaty; fighting stopped in 1953 with an armistice.
Pyongyang's Ryugyong Hotel, begun in 1987, has never fully opened.
